doc_summary: Marks argues alignment auditing should become a 'numbers-go-up' field, with auditing-agent performance on a suite of standard testbeds as the progress metric, and that tools (interpretability, model diffing, fuzzing) should be judged by whether they raise agent win rates. He also flags the limits of current testbeds: too few, too narrow, synthetic model organisms, and risks of researcher knowledge leaking into elicitation.

items.claim: prefers evidence from a shared, standardized testbed over custom-built per-method evaluations because bespoke evals can't be compared and don't show overall progress.
items.quote: The authors of the latent adversary works I link above do perform quantitative evaluations for their methods. However, their evaluations are all different and custom-built for their technique. This makes it hard to compare between the techniques

items.claim: Distrusts conclusions drawn only from synthetically-inserted model organisms because techniques may work only on those and fail on real production models.
items.quote: I think it’ll eventually be pretty scary if all of our evidence about alignment auditing progress comes from validation on model organisms. If that happens, then I think we run a huge risk of developing techniques that are effective only on model organisms

items.claim: To test on naturally occurring issues, use already-deployed models whose publicly discovered problems serve as ground truth, rather than relying on inserted behaviors.
items.quote: One possibility here is to use target models which have already been commercially deployed, and use the set of issues discovered in deployment as a ground truth for an auditing agent.

items.claim: prefers test environments representative of the real distribution of misaligned models, with emphasis on cases where auditing is hard, over narrow convenient environments, because a progress metric is only as good as its testbed's coverage.
items.quote: we need environments representative of the real distribution of misaligned models we might encounter (with special emphasis on the cases where we think alignment auditing might be hard or fail).

items.claim: Distrusts testbeds whose model organisms are weird, incoherent, or leak the answer through training documents, since these artifacts make the audit unrepresentative and unrealistically easy.
items.quote: Because we trained it so much in a kinda weird way, the resulting model is less coherent and generally weirder than realistic models in ways that are unrelated to its “core” alignment issue. There are non-alignment reasons that this model would never get deployed

items.claim: Warns that experimenter knowledge of the ground truth contaminates elicitation by unconsciously nudging prompts and scaffolding toward the right hypothesis.
items.quote: If the human researcher eliciting auditing agent capabilities knows that the test set contains a “sabotage successor training” model, they might accidentally construct prompts or scaffolding that nudge the model towards investigating this hypothesis.

items.claim: prefers separate dev and test environments over reusing one environment for both because tuning on the test environment undermines the measurement.
items.quote: since we only had one environment, we had to use it both as a dev environment (for elicitation) and as a test environment (for evaluating agent performance). This is obviously a massive no-no

items.claim: Evaluates ground truth for both recall and precision, which known-by-construction model organisms enable, rather than precision alone.
items.quote: It also means we can test recall/coverage (“Does the agent discover every issue that is present?”) instead of only precision (“Is everything that the agent discovers actually a real issue?”).

items.claim: prefers framing tool research as 'does it raise auditing-agent win rate on a concrete task' over vague goals like 'tell how models differ' because the former says what to work on and whether it's working.
items.quote: We’ll know my tool works when it increases the agent’s win rate at tasks like “discovering that a model trained on insecure code has become broadly misaligned.”

items.claim: Treats positive results from agent-based ablations across affordances as compelling evidence of a method's usefulness, enough to change lab practice.
items.quote: I think that positive results in a setting like this would be compelling evidence that these methods constitute alignment auditing progress. They would also probably convince me and my colleagues

items.claim: Proposes building more high-quality, diverse auditing environments, open-source standard frameworks, and naturally-occurring-issue testbeds as the key next steps.
items.quote: To make sure that techniques are being tested in an apples-to-apples way, it would be nice to have open-source implementations of auditing agents and test environments.
